heroData.title: EOR & PEO in Yemen
heroData.subtitle: Hire compliant teams in Yemen without a local entity
heroData.description: Navigate Yemen's complex labor market with an Employer of Record. Ensure compliance with the Labor Code (Act No. 5), manage residence visas for expats, and handle strict termination protections while you focus on operations.
heroData.bestFor: NGOs, construction firms, and tech companies entering the market

steps.title: Ministry Approval & Quota Check
steps.description: For foreign hires, the EOR must secure approval from the Ministry of Social Affairs and Labour, ensuring the total workforce does not exceed the 10% non-Yemeni quota.

steps.title: Tripartite Contract Signing
steps.description: Drafting the employment contract in three copies (one for the Ministry). Contracts must specify wages, benefits, and comply with the 48-hour work week limit.

steps.title: Work Permit & Residence Visa
steps.description: The EOR sponsors the Work Permit and subsequent Residence Visa. This ties the employee's legal status directly to the EOR entity.

steps.title: Social Security Registration
steps.description: Registering the employee for social insurance (GOSI), covering pension and disability. Employer contributes 9% and pays 1% for vocational training.

steps.title: Ministry Registry
steps.description: Within two weeks of the start date, the EOR records the new hire's details in the specific company register as mandated by labor regulations.

items.title: Arbitrary Dismissal Protections
items.text: Yemen law strictly prohibits arbitrary dismissal. Compensation for wrongful termination is determined by an Arbitration Committee and can reach up to 6 months of wages.

items.title: Probationary Limits
items.text: Probation periods are capped at 6 months. During this time, either party can terminate without notice, but this period cannot be repeated for the same role.

items.title: Written Contracts Mandatory
items.text: Verbal agreements are risky. The Labor Code explicitly requires written contracts filed with the Ministry to be enforceable and to protect employer rights.

faqs.question: What is the notice period for termination?
faqs.answer: For monthly salaried employees, the statutory notice period is 30 days. For those paid less frequently, it can be 15 days or 1 week, but 30 days is the standard best practice.

faqs.question: How is severance pay calculated?
faqs.answer: Severance is mandatory for lawful termination: 1/2 month's wage per year for the first 5 years, and 1 full month's wage for each subsequent year.

faqs.question: Can I hire anyone in Yemen?
faqs.answer: You can hire Yemeni nationals freely. For expats, you are limited to a 10% quota of your total workforce and must prove local talent is unavailable.

items.title: Islamic Holidays
items.text: Working hours are often reduced by 2 hours per day during the holy month of Ramadan. Eid breaks are significant public holidays.

items.title: End-of-Service Gratuity
items.text: Even if not explicitly stated in a contract, the Labor Code guarantees end-of-service benefits, making them an unavoidable accrual cost.

items.title: Cash vs Bank Transfer
items.text: While bank transfers are preferred for compliance, cash payments via approved exchange houses are common due to banking infrastructure challenges.

steps.title: Eligibility Check
steps.description: Employees not covered by the Social Insurance Act are entitled to severance under Article 120 of the Labor Code.

steps.title: Base Calculation
steps.description: The statutory minimum is one full month's wage for each year of service. Fractions of a year are calculated proportionally.

steps.title: Wage Basis
steps.description: The calculation must based on the 'last received wage', including all stable allowances, not just the basic salary.

steps.title: Resignation vs Termination
steps.description: Voluntary resignation may reduce entitlement depending on tenure (e.g., <2 years), whereas arbitrary termination guarantees full payout plus compensation.

steps.title: Gross Pay Calculation
steps.description: Aggregating base salary, overtime (1.5x standard rate), and allowances (housing, transport) before deductions.

steps.title: Social Security Deduction
steps.description: Withholding 6% from the employee's gross pay for GCSS. The employer calculates their 9% contribution simultaneously.

steps.title: Income Tax (PAYE) Calculation
steps.description: Applying the progressive tax rates (0%, 10%, 15%) after deducting the allowable social security contribution and standard allowances.

steps.title: Remittance to Authorities
steps.description: Paying withheld Income Tax by the 10th and Social Security contributions by the 15th of the following month.

steps.title: Net Pay Disbursement
steps.description: Transferring net salaries to employee bank accounts or authorized exchange houses (due to banking limitations) by month-end.

items.title: Resident Tax Brackets
items.text: First 120,000 YER is exempt. 120,001-240,000 YER is taxed at 10%. Amounts above 240,000 YER are taxed at 15%.

items.title: Remittance Deadlines
items.text: Strict deadlines apply: 10th of the month for Income Tax and 15th for Social Security. Late payments attract fines.

items.title: Deductible Allowances
items.text: Employees can deduct their 6% social security contribution and a standard allowance (up to 65,000 YER cap) before tax calculation.

faqs.question: What is the standard payroll frequency?
faqs.answer: Monthly is the standard frequency. Paying less frequently is generally not compliant with the Labor Code.

faqs.question: Are expats subject to Social Security?
faqs.answer: Yes, foreign employees must also contribute 6% to the GCSS, and employers pay their share. Expats can claim a lump sum refund upon permanent departure (minus service fees).

faqs.question: How are overtime rates calculated?
faqs.answer: Overtime is typically paid at 150% (1.5x) of the normal hourly wage for standard overtime hours, and higher for public holidays.

items.title: Banking Infrastructure
items.text: Due to liquidity issues in local banks, many companies use recognized exchange houses (like Al-Kurimi) for salary disbursement.

items.title: Currency Split
items.text: In practice, some expat salaries are paid in USD abroad, but tax must be calculated on the local equivalent and paid in YER.

items.title: E-Filing
items.text: While manual filing is still common, larger taxpayers are increasingly encouraged to use electronic reporting where available.

items.title: Overtime Multiplier
items.text: Standard overtime is paid at 150% (1.5x) of the normal hourly rate. Work performed on Friday or public holidays requires a higher premium or compensatory time off.

items.title: 13th Month Pay
items.text: While not legally mandated, a '13th Month' bonus is a widespread custom, often paid before Eid al-Fitr to support employees' holiday expenses.

items.title: Allowance Tax
items.text: Housing and transport allowances are generally taxable unless specifically exempted under strict documentation proving they are 'reimbursements' rather than income.

steps.title: Employer Social Security
steps.description: 9% to 11% of gross salary. This covers retirement, disability, and work injury insurance managed by the General Corporation for Social Security (GCSS).

steps.title: Employee Social Security
steps.description: 6% to 7% of gross salary. Deducted at source by the employer.

steps.title: Income Tax
steps.description: Progressive rates from 10% to 20% for residents. Non-residents are taxed at a flat 20% rate.

steps.title: Zakat
steps.description: A 2.5% Zakat tax applies to net revenue/commercial profits, collected by the state.

steps.title: Skills Training Fund
steps.description: Employers may be liable for a 1% contribution to the Skills Development Fund, though enforcement depends on the jurisdiction.

items.title: Currency Volatility
items.text: The Yemeni Rial (YER) rate fluctuates significantly between Sana'a and Aden. Payroll budgets should account for exchange rate risks if funding in USD.

items.title: End of Service Gratuity
items.text: Mandatory strictly for contracts where no social security is paid, but often expected. Typically 1 month's salary per year of service.

items.title: Net vs Gross
items.text: Negotiations often focus on Net Salary. Ensure you gross-up correctly to include the ~6-7% employee deduction and tax.

faqs.question: What is the 13th month pay?
faqs.answer: It is not a statutory requirement in Yemen, but performance bonuses or Eid bonuses are common cultural expectations.

faqs.question: How often must tax be remitted?
faqs.answer: Payroll taxes and social security contributions must be remitted monthly, typically within the first 10-15 days of the following month.

faqs.question: Is insurance mandatory?
faqs.answer: Private health insurance is not mandatory by law but is a highly valued benefit due to the poor state of public healthcare.

items.title: Late Filing Penalty
items.text: Failure to file tax returns on time incurs a penalty of 2% of the tax payable for every month of delay.

items.title: Evasion Fines
items.text: Proven tax evasion applies a penalty of 100% to 150% of the evaded amount, plus potentially imprisonment for up to 3 years.

items.title: Loss-Making Entities
items.text: Even if no tax is due (loss-making), late filing attracts a flat fine ranging from 200,000 to 5,000,000 YER depending on entity type.

items.title: Religious Tax (Zakat)
items.text: Zakat is mandatory for businesses at a rate of 2.5% of net revenue or 'zakatable assets' (stock, raw materials). It is collected by the Zakat Authority.

items.title: Asset Exemptions
items.text: Fixed assets used for production (buildings, machinery, fleet vehicles) are generally exempt from the Zakat base.

items.title: Double Taxation
items.text: Businesses must pay both Zakat (2.5%) and Corporate Income Tax (20%). Ensure your financial planning accounts for this dual burden.

heroData.title: Incorporation in Yemen
heroData.subtitle: Set up your Limited Liability Company (LLC) or Branch
heroData.description: A complete guide to legal entity registration in Yemen. Understand the costs, timelines, and capitalization requirements to establish a fully compliant local presence.
heroData.bestFor: Long-term market entry and government contracting

sections.title: Entity Registration Workflow
sections.subtitle: From name reservation to trade license

steps.title: Trade Name Reservation
steps.description: Apply at the Commercial Register (Ministry of Industry & Trade) to reserve a unique company name. Usually takes 1 working day.

steps.title: Capital Deposit & Bank Certificate
steps.description: Deposit the minimum capital (YER 1,000,000 for LLC) in a local bank blocked account and obtain a bank certificate as proof.

steps.title: Commercial Registration
steps.description: Submit Articles of Association (AoA), Memorandum of Association (MoA), and shareholder docs to validte the entity. Includes publication in the official gazette.

steps.title: Tax & Chamber Membership
steps.description: Register with the General Taxes Department for a TIN and join the Chamber of Commerce, mandatory for obtaining the final business license.

steps.title: Final Municipality License
steps.description: Obtain the Commercial License from the local Municipality/Zakat office to legally commence operations.

items.title: Local Management
items.text: While 100% foreign ownership is allowed, appointing a Yemeni national as the General Manager is often practically required for smooth interaction with government bodies.

items.title: Timeframe Reality
items.text: Official timelines suggest ~40 days, but administrative delays can extend this to 2-3 months. Document legalization abroad (Embassy) adds significant time.

items.title: Branch vs LLC
items.text: LLCs are preferred for liability protection. Branches are allowed but require Ministry of Economy approval and are subject to stricter scrutiny.

faqs.question: Can foreigners own 100% of the company?
faqs.answer: Yes, Yemen's Investment Law allows 100% foreign ownership in most sectors, excluding banking, insurance, and commercial agencies.

faqs.question: What documents require legalization?
faqs.answer: Foreign corporate documents (AoA, MoA, Board Resolutions) must be notarized, certified by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in the home country, and legalized by the Yemeni Embassy (approx $120/doc).

faqs.question: Is a physical office required?
faqs.answer: Yes, a registered office address is mandatory. A lease agreement is required for the Municipality License application.

items.title: Tax Holiday
items.text: Entities registered in the AFZ benefit from a 15-year exemption on profit and income taxes, extendable by another 10 years based on employment and export criteria.

items.title: 100% Ownership
items.text: Unlike mainland entities, Free Zone companies allow 100% foreign ownership without the need for a local Yemeni partner.

items.title: Duty Exemptions
items.text: Goods imported into the zone for manufacturing or re-export are exempt from all customs duties and import fees.

heroData.title: Staffing & Recruitment in Yemen
heroData.subtitle: Find and hire top local and expatriate talent
heroData.description: Navigate Yemen's recruitment landscape with compliant staffing strategies. Understand agency fees, fixed-term vs. indefinite contracts, and the strict 10% foreigner quota.
heroData.bestFor: Projects requiring specialized technical skills or rapid scaling

steps.title: Sourcing & Screening
steps.description: Leveraging local networks and recognized agencies. Direct sourcing is common, but 'referral hiring' remains a dominant channel in Yemen.

steps.title: Quota Verification
steps.description: Ensuring the role fits within the 10% foreign national quota if hiring expats. Ministry approval is required for exceeding this limit.

steps.title: Contract Issuance
steps.description: Drafting a written contract (Fixed-term or Indefinite) in Arabic. Three copies are required: for the employer, employee, and Ministry.

steps.title: Work Permit Processing
steps.description: For foreign hires, the employer sponsors the Work Permit application, submitting medical checks and police clearance certificates.

steps.title: Onboarding & Registration
steps.description: Registering the new hire for Social Security (GCSS) and recording their details in the company's internal labor register.

items.title: Fixed-Term Renewal Risk
items.text: Repeated renewal of fixed-term contracts can legally convert them into indefinite contracts, granting the employee full protection against arbitrary dismissal.

items.title: Probation Period
items.text: Maximum 6 months. During this period, termination is permitted without notice or severance, but it cannot be repeated for the same role.

items.title: Written Contracts
items.text: Always issue written contracts. While verbal agreements are valid, they are difficult to defend in Labor Courts, which tend to favor the employee.

faqs.question: Can I hire foreign workers freely?
faqs.answer: No, you are generally limited to 10% of your total workforce. Exceptions exist for specialized skills unavailable in the local market, subject to Ministry approval.

faqs.question: Are background checks legal?
faqs.answer: Yes, requesting criminal records (Police Clearance) and medical certificates is standard practice, especially for foreign hires.

faqs.question: What is the notice period during probation?
faqs.answer: Legally, no notice is strictly required during probation, but contracts often stipulate a short period (e.g., 2-7 days) as a courtesy.

items.title: Campus Partnerships
items.text: Partnering with Sana'a University or Aden University for graduate programs is a strategic way to access top entry-level talent in engineering and IT.

items.title: Quota Relief
items.text: The Ministry often views training programs for fresh graduates favorably when assessing requests for expatriate quota exceptions.

items.title: Skills Gap
items.text: While theoretical knowledge is strong, practical skills may require internal investment. Budget for a 3-month intensive onboarding/training phase.

heroData.title: HRIS in Yemen
heroData.subtitle: Digitize your Yemeni workforce records
heroData.description: Manage employee data, leave tracking, and document compliance in Yemen. Ensure secure storage of contracts and wage receipts while navigating emerging data privacy regulations.

steps.title: Data Migration & Audit
steps.description: Digitizing physical employee files, ensuring all mandatory documents (signed contracts, IDs, medical checks) are present.

steps.title: Localization Setup
steps.description: Configuring the system for Yemen's workweek (Sunday-Thursday), public holidays, and Arabic language interface if needed for local staff.

steps.title: Access Control Configuration
steps.description: Implementing role-based access to comply with Law No. 13 of 2012 regarding the confidentiality of personal data.

steps.title: Document Repository Initiation
steps.description: Creating secure digital folders for 'Triple Copy' contract storage and scanned monthly wage receipts (signed/fingerprinted).

steps.title: Training & Rollout
steps.description: Training staff on self-service portals for leave requests and payslip access, ensuring mobile compatibility for reliable access.

items.title: Physical Backup Required
items.text: While digital records are efficient, Yemeni Labor Courts heavily rely on physical, signed/stamped paper documents for dispute resolution. Maintain a hybrid system.

items.title: Privacy Regulation
items.text: Yemen lacks a GDPR-equivalent, but the Constitution and Law No. 13 of 2012 mandate that personal data cannot be shared without consent. Secure cloud storage is essential.

items.title: Wage Receipt Tracking
items.text: The Labor Code considers the employer's wage obligation fulfilled only upon the worker's signature/fingerprint. An HRIS should track who has physically signed their pay slip.

items.title: Connectivity Issues
items.text: Internet stability in Yemen can be intermittent. Offline-first capabilities or low-bandwidth modes are critical for local HRIS access.

items.title: Calendar Synchronization
items.text: Ensure your system accurately reflects religious holidays (Eid, Ramadan hours) which shift annually based on the lunar calendar.

items.title: Foreign Worker Register
items.text: Automate alerts for visa and work permit expiries. The Ministry requires an up-to-date register of all foreign employees.

faqs.question: Is cloud storage legal for HR data?
faqs.answer: There is no specific prohibition against off-shore cloud storage, provided data confidentiality is maintained in line with constitutional privacy rights.

faqs.question: What records must be retained?
faqs.answer: There is no statutory retention period, but best practice is to keep wage records, contracts, and medical files for at least 5 years post-termination to defend against claims.

faqs.question: Do I need Arabic software?
faqs.answer: While not legally mandated for internal tools, using Arabic interfaces improves adoption among local staff and ensures clarity in policy communication.

steps.title: Inventory Audit
steps.description: Cataloging all physical personnel files. Identify missing documents (IDs, contracts, medical reports) before scanning.

steps.title: Scanning & OCR
steps.description: Scanning all 'wet ink' signed documents at high resolution. Using OCR for Arabic text is improving but manual metadata tagging is recommended.

steps.title: Secure Cloud Upload
steps.description: Uploading encrypted files to a redundant cloud storage solution. Ensure server locations comply with any client-specific data sovereignty clauses.

steps.title: Access Logging
steps.description: Implementing strict audit logs. You must know who accessed an employee's personal file and when to comply with privacy norms.

steps.title: Physical Archive
steps.description: Do not destroy originals. Store them in a fireproof, secure local facility as they are the primary evidence in Labor Court disputes.

heroData.title: Accounting in Yemen
heroData.subtitle: IFRS-compliant bookkeeping and financial reporting
heroData.description: Manage your financial records in adherence to Council of Ministers Resolution No. 51. Ensure compliance with IFRS standards for large entities and keep audit-ready books in Yemen's challenging economic landscape.

steps.title: Bookkeeping Setup
steps.description: Establishing a Chart of Accounts compliant with IFRS disclosure requirements. Transactions should be recorded in Yemeni Rial (YER) for statutory purposes.

steps.title: Audit Preparation
steps.description: Compiling financial statements (Balance Sheet, P&L, Cash Flow) for the fiscal year ending December 31st. Large taxpayers must engage a YACPA-certified auditor.

steps.title: Tax Declaration Filing
steps.description: Submitting the Corporate Income Tax declaration and audited financials to the Tax Authority within 120 days of the year-end (typically by April 30th).

steps.title: Record Archiving
steps.description: Archiving all financial documents, ledgers, and supporting vouchers for the mandatory 10-year retention period.

steps.title: Chamber Renewal
steps.description: Using the audited financials to renew membership with the Chamber of Commerce, a prerequisite for renewing the commercial license.

items.title: IFRS Mandate
items.text: Since 2020, full IFRS is mandatory for banks and large entities (revenue > 200M YER). SMEs can use 'IFRS for SMEs'. There is no separate local GAAP.

items.title: Currency Fluctuations
items.text: The divergence between the official exchange rate and the parallel market rate requires careful accounting treatment for foreign currency transactions to strictly comply with Central Bank guidelines.

items.title: Auditor Selection
items.text: Ensure your appointed auditor is a member of the Yemeni Association of Certified Public Accountants (YACPA) to guarantee acceptance by the Tax Authority.

items.title: 10-Year Rule
items.text: Financial books and accounting records must be preserved for 10 years. This long period is strictly enforced during tax audits.

items.title: Physical Copies
items.text: Digital archives are good for backup, but authorities typically demand original hard copies of vouchers and invoices during inspections.

items.title: Fiscal Year
items.text: The standard fiscal year is January 1st to December 31st. Deviations require special approval from the Tax Authority.

faqs.question: What is the filing deadline?
faqs.answer: The deadline for filing corporate tax returns and audited financial statements is April 30th (120 days after the standard Dec 31st fiscal year end).

faqs.question: Can I keep books in USD?
faqs.answer: While internal management accounts can be in any currency, statutory books filed with the Yemeni government must be presented in Yemeni Rial (YER).

faqs.question: Is an audit mandatory?
faqs.answer: Yes, for all limited liability companies and corporations. Tax authorities require certified audited statements to accept the declared tax liability.

steps.title: AML/KYC Verification
steps.description: Complying with Law No. 1/2010 by identifying legitimate beneficiaries and retaining customer data for at least 5 years.

steps.title: Employee Background Checks
steps.description: Mandatory age verification using birth certificates or national IDs to prevent child labor. Work permit sponsorship acts as a government-level background check for expats.

steps.title: Conflict of Interest
steps.description: Establishing internal policies to prevent conflicts, especially given the lack of robust external whistleblowing protections in the Anti-Corruption Law.

steps.title: Sanctions Screening
steps.description: Due to the sensitive geopolitical situation, enhanced due diligence is required to ensure no funds or resources benefit sanctioned entities or individuals.

steps.title: Financial Reporting
steps.description: Reporting suspicious transactions to the Financial Information Unit (FIU) regarding potential money laundering or terrorism financing activities.

items.title: Whistleblowing Gap
items.text: Yemen lacks a dedicated whistleblower protection law. Companies should implement internal anonymous reporting channels to mitigate corruption risks without relying solely on state mechanisms.

items.title: Data Privacy
items.text: Draft Law No. 13 of 2012 generally protects personal data. Background checks must be relevant to the role and respect constitutional privacy rights.

items.title: Corruption Index
items.text: Yemen often ranks low on global corruption indices. Strict internal audit controls and 'zero-tolerance' policies are essential for international compliance.

items.title: Central Bank of Yemen
items.text: The primary regulator for financial compliance, overseeing banking sector adherence to AML/CFT standards.

items.title: Anti-Corruption Authority
items.text: The Supreme National Authority for Combating Corruption (SNACC) is the body designated to receive corruption reports, though enforcement can be inconsistent.

items.title: Local vs. International
items.text: International companies must often balance local compliance with stricter home-country regulations (e.g., FCPA, UK Bribery Act) due to the high-risk environment.

faqs.question: Are background checks legal?
faqs.answer: Yes, verifying identity, age, and criminal record (via Police Clearance Certificate) is standard practice, especially for foreign hires during the work permit process.

faqs.question: What is the AML retention period?
faqs.answer: Financial records and customer identification documents must be retained for at least 5 years to comply with AML/CFT regulations.

faqs.question: Can I transfer data offshore?
faqs.answer: There is no strict data residency law prohibiting it, but ensuring data security and confidentiality is a legal obligation under civil and constitutional law.

steps.title: Dividends
steps.description: 10% WHT for non-resident companies. 0% for resident companies if the underlying profit was already taxed.

steps.title: Interest Payments
steps.description: 10% WHT for non-residents. 0% for payments to approved foreign banks or resident companies.

steps.title: Royalties & Technical Fees
steps.description: 10% WHT applies to royalties, patent fees, and technical service payments made to non-resident entities.

steps.title: Remittance Procedures
steps.description: WHT must be deducted at source and remitted to the Tax Authority within 15 days of the payment date.

items.title: Double Taxation Agreements
items.text: Yemen has DTA treaties with countries including UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Jordan, Egypt, and Turkey to prevent double taxation.

items.title: Conflict Impact
items.text: Due to the political situation, enforcing treaty benefits can be complex. The tax administration is currently divided, leading to potential dual taxation risks in practice.

items.title: Capital Gains
items.text: Capital gains are treated as ordinary income and taxed at the standard 20% CIT rate. Non-residents selling Yemeni shares are also subject to this 20% tax.

faqs.question: Is there VAT in Yemen?
faqs.answer: No, Yemen operates a General Sales Tax (GST) system with a standard rate of 5%. It is not a value-added tax with input credit mechanisms in the traditional sense.

faqs.question: When is the tax year?
faqs.answer: The fiscal year is the calendar year (Jan 1 - Dec 31). Returns must be filed within 120 days of year-end (by April 30th).

faqs.question: Are there tax incentives?
faqs.answer: Yes, projects under the Investment Law benefit from a reduced 15% CIT rate and customs duty exemptions on imported capital goods.

steps.title: Threshold Assessment
steps.description: Businesses with annual turnover exceeding 50 Million YER (approx $95k USD at official rate) must register for GST.

steps.title: TIN Application
steps.description: Obtain a Tax Identification Number from the Yemen Tax Authority. This unique ID tracks all CIT and GST payments.

steps.title: Monthly Filing
steps.description: GST declarations must be filed monthly by the 21st of the following month. Late filings attract penalties.

steps.title: Telecom Surcharge
steps.description: Note that while standard goods are 5%, telecommunications and mobile services attract a higher 10% rate.

heroData.title: Contracts in Yemen
heroData.subtitle: Drafting enforceable service agreements
heroData.description: Secure your business relationships in Yemen. Understand the validity of electronic signatures under Law No. 13 of 2006, dual-language contract requirements, and intellectual property assignment for employee inventions.

steps.title: Dual-Language Requirement
steps.description: Contracts should be drafted in Arabic or be bilingual. In case of dispute, the Arabic text prevails in Yemeni courts.

steps.title: Defined Scope & Payment
steps.description: Clearly articulating the 'Scope of Services' and 'Payment Terms' is vital to avoid ambiguity, as Yemeni civil law is less detailed on implied terms.

steps.title: Termination Clauses
steps.description: Explicitly stating notice periods and termination conditions (cause vs. convenience) is essential to limit liability.

steps.title: IP Assignment
steps.description: Under Decree No. 19 of 1994, employers own inventions created during employment, but the contract should specify remuneration to avoid disputes.

steps.title: Dispute Resolution
steps.description: Specifying arbitration or mediation is recommended over litigation due to the complex and sometimes unpredictable nature of the local court system.

items.title: Electronic Signatures
items.text: Law No. 13 of 2006 validates electronic signatures, but 'wet' signatures are still safer for high-value contracts or those requiring notarization.

items.title: Governing Law
items.text: While foreign governing law can be chosen, it may be set aside by Yemeni courts if deemed contrary to Sharia public policy principles.

items.title: Triple Copies
items.text: Always execute contracts in at least three original copies (Employer, Employee/Vendor, Government/File) to satisfy administrative requirements.

faqs.question: Are e-signatures legal?
faqs.answer: Yes, they are legally recognized under the Electronic Transactions Law, provided they meet reliability criteria (unique to signer, under their control).

faqs.question: Can I use English contracts?
faqs.answer: You can, but a certified Arabic translation will be required for any court proceedings or government filing.

faqs.question: Who owns employee IP?
faqs.answer: Generally the employer, if the invention relates to the employee's duties. However, the law entitles the employee to fair remuneration, which should be defined in the MSA.

items.title: Legal Recognition
items.text: Under Law No. 13 of 2006, electronic signatures are legally binding if they meet 'reliability' criteria, meaning they are uniquely linked to the signatory and created under their sole control.

items.title: Enforceability Risks
items.text: For a digital contract to be enforceable, both parties must explicitly consent to the electronic format. 'Wet' signatures are still recommended for high-risk or government contracts.

items.title: Tamper Evidence
items.text: The signing system must be capable of detecting any alteration to the document after the signature is applied to be admissible in Yemeni courts.

items.title: Embassy Certification
items.text: Certifying commercial documents at a Yemeni Embassy abroad typically costs ~$120 USD per document. Personal documents are lower (~$60).

items.title: Online Notarization
items.text: Services like Notarize.com can suffice for initial verifications at ~$25/doc, but final use in Yemen often requires the full consular legalization chain.

items.title: Ministry of Justice
items.text: Local authentication within Yemen is affordable (nominal fees in YER), but the process involves physical queues and bureaucratic delays.

heroData.title: Software in Yemen
heroData.subtitle: Building for low-bandwidth environments
heroData.description: Navigate Yemen's digital landscape characterized by slow internet (avg. <4 Mbps), high costs, and infrastructure challenges. Learn how to deploy offline-first solutions effectively.
heroData.bestFor: Tech companies and digital health/aid providers

steps.title: Bandwidth Optimization
steps.description: Prioritize text-based interfaces and compression. Yemen has some of the slowest internet speeds globally (often <1 Mbps upload).

steps.title: Offline-First Architecture
steps.description: Ensure core functionalities work without a connection. Frequent outages due to power cuts and cable damage are common.

steps.title: SMS & USSD Integration
steps.description: Leverage basic mobile protocols (SMS/USSD) for reaching wider users, as smartphone penetration is lower than regional averages.

steps.title: Local Hosting vs. Cloud
steps.description: While no data residency law exists, banking apps often prefer local hosting. For others, regional GCC cloud regions offer the best latency.

steps.title: Security Hardening
steps.description: With limited national cybersecurity infrastructure, private actors must implement robust encryption and endpoint protection.

items.title: Infrastructure Risk
items.text: Reliance on the single FALCON subsea cable creates a single point of failure. Internet blackouts can last days. Satellite internet (e.g., Starlink) is being explored but regulatory status is fluid.

items.title: Cost Barrier
items.text: Internet costs can consume up to 10% of average income. B2C apps must be extremely lightweight to avoid draining user data plans.

items.title: Talent Pool
items.text: There is a nascent but eager developer community. However, 'brain drain' is an issue. Remote firms offering USD salaries have a massive competitive advantage.

faqs.question: Is 4G available?
faqs.answer: Yes, but coverage is spotty and fragmented between different providers (YemenNet vs. AdenNet). Speeds are generally well below global 4G standards.

faqs.question: Are there data localization laws?
faqs.answer: Currently, there is no comprehensive GDPR-style law mandating local data storage, though financial services regulations are stricter.

faqs.question: How reliable is power for servers?
faqs.answer: Public grid power is virtually non-existent in many areas. Any local physical infrastructure must rely on independent solar or generator backup.

heroData.title: Marketing in Yemen
heroData.subtitle: Navigating cultural sensitivities
heroData.description: Reach Yemeni audiences effectively by respecting Islamic values and leveraging the dominant channels: Arabic-language social media (Facebook) and satellite TV.

steps.title: Cultural Compliance
steps.description: Strict adherence to Islamic values is non-negotiable. Avoid alcohol, gambling, and immodest imagery. Men and women should be depicted modestly.

steps.title: Language Localization
steps.description: Arabic is mandatory for widespread reach. English consumption is low outside the business elite. Dialect usage (Yemeni Arabic) boosts engagement.

steps.title: Channel Selection
steps.description: Satellite TV (Al-Jazeera, Al-Arabiya, local channels) remains a primary news source. Facebook is the dominant social platform (~5.3M users).

steps.title: Influencer Engagement
steps.description: Micro-influencers on Facebook and YouTube are growing in trust. However, vet them carefully for political neutrality.

steps.title: Indirect Communication
steps.description: Messaging should be respectful and indirect. Hard-sell tactics or direct comparisons with competitors can be viewed negatively.

items.title: Censorship
items.text: The Ministry of Information controls most traditional media. Content is monitored for political and religious alignment. Avoid politically sensitive topics.

items.title: Consumer Protection
items.text: Law No. 46 of 2008 grants consumers the 'right to be informed'. Misleading advertising can lead to penalties, though enforcement varies.

items.title: Social Commerce
items.text: WhatsApp groups are heavily used for informal commerce and community updates. Marketing via direct messaging lists is common but requires permission.

faqs.question: Are there specific ad bans?
faqs.answer: Yes, alcohol, pork products, gambling, and anything deemed offensive to Islamic morality are strictly prohibited.

faqs.question: Do I need a license to advertise?
faqs.answer: Generally, media outlets (TV, Print) require licenses to operate. As an advertiser, you must ensure your agency adheres to Ministry of Information regulations.

faqs.question: What is the internet penetration?
faqs.answer: Approx. 17.7% (6.16 million users) as of early 2024. While low, it is concentrated in urban centers which are key markets.

items.title: Youth Bulge
items.text: Approximately 60% of the population is under the age of 25. Marketing campaigns should appeal to youth aspirations, education, and technology.

items.title: Mobile First
items.text: With limited desktop penetration, all digital assets must be optimized for mobile screens. Short-form video content is highly consumable.

items.title: Community Values
items.text: Yemeni society is deeply family-oriented and conservative. Messaging that emphasizes community, family stability, and tradition resonates best.
